To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the processing of emotional stimuli in visual cortex is under attentional control and (2) attentional control is not limited to the processing of emotional information but extends to the processing of any category of information.
(1) the processing of emotional stimuli is attention-dependent and (2) attention can modulate activity in visual cortex in the absence of stimulation.

the neural processing (as reflected in brain activation) of stimuli with emotional valence (i.e., facial expressions of fear and happiness) requires some degree of visual attention, and that this attentional control is exerted by a distributed network of frontal and parieto-temporal brain regions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of selective attention and their neural implementation in visual processing.
the mechanisms that underlie the selection of relevant information from the environment.
the neural mechanisms of selective attention and the processing of emotional stimuli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural processing is not automatic, but it is modulated by attentional control, and the degree to which this is true depends on the stimulus category.
emotional stimuli, like all other stimuli, require attention for their processing, and that the processing of all stimuli can be modulated by top-down attention.
attentional control is a general mechanism for modulating neural processing, which applies to the processing of emotional stimuli as well as to other stimulus categories.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural representation of a stimulus is a product of bottom-up sensory input and top-down attentional control.
the processing of emotional and other types of stimuli is subject to attentional control, which is implemented by a network of frontal and parieto-temporal areas.
attention is a necessary but not sufficient factor to elicit emotional responses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, contrary to what has been assumed, emotional stimuli do not activate brain regions "automaticall," but instead require some degree of attentional control.
attentional control is a general property of neural representation, not limited to specific stimulus categories.
the processing of all stimuli, even those with emotional content, depends on the availability of attentional resources.
